scope: General Medicare rules stated from Medicare.gov, for the invite-only Collier pilot. Each statement is a general rule with its conditions; none is a personal eligibility finding, date or amount for a specific person. Proposed by the November 8 review and accepted by the owner the same day (D109).

facts.title: Job coverage and delaying Part B
facts.question: Can someone with job insurance delay Part B?
facts.text: If someone has health insurance from their own or a spouse's current job and the employer has 20 or more employees, that job coverage pays first and they can usually delay Part B without a late-enrollment penalty. When the job or that coverage ends, a Special Enrollment Period lets them sign up for Part B during the 8 months that follow. Part A is premium-free for most people and is often taken at 65 even when Part B is delayed. The employer size and whether the coverage is based on current employment are what decide this; COBRA and retiree coverage do not count as current employment.
facts.summary: With current-job coverage from an employer of 20 or more, Part B can usually be delayed; an 8-month sign-up window opens when that coverage ends.

facts.title: Health savings accounts and Medicare
facts.question: What happens to an HSA when Medicare starts?
facts.text: Once any part of Medicare begins, including premium-free Part A, a person can no longer contribute to a Health Savings Account. Part A enrollment can also be backdated up to 6 months, so people who contribute to an HSA often stop contributions before applying. Money already in the account can still be used.
facts.summary: HSA contributions must stop when Medicare starts; Part A can be backdated up to 6 months.

facts.title: The Medicare Advantage trial right
facts.question: Can someone who joined Medicare Advantage switch to Medigap?
facts.text: Someone who joined a Medicare Advantage plan when they first became eligible at 65 has a trial right: if they leave that plan within the first 12 months, they can buy a Medigap policy with guaranteed issue, meaning the insurer cannot refuse them or charge more because of their health. Outside that trial right and the 6-month Medigap Open Enrollment Period that starts with Part B at 65 or older, an insurer can usually ask health questions and may decline or charge more. Leaving Medicare Advantage also means returning to Original Medicare and choosing a separate Part D plan.
facts.summary: Leaving a first Medicare Advantage plan within 12 months of joining at 65 gives a guaranteed right to buy Medigap.

facts.title: The Part D late-enrollment penalty
facts.question: Is there a penalty for going without drug coverage?
facts.text: Medicare adds a Part D late-enrollment penalty when someone goes 63 or more days in a row without Medicare drug coverage or other creditable drug coverage after their first chance to enroll. The penalty is about 1% of the national base premium for each month without coverage, added to the monthly premium for as long as the person has Medicare drug coverage. People who qualify for Extra Help do not pay the penalty. Someone with Original Medicare can add a stand-alone Part D plan without changing to Medicare Advantage.
facts.summary: Going 63 or more days without creditable drug coverage adds about 1% per month to the Part D premium for life; Extra Help removes the penalty.

facts.title: Extra Help with drug costs
facts.question: Is there help with Medicare drug costs for people with limited income?
facts.text: Extra Help is a Medicare program for people with limited income and resources. It pays most of the Part D premium and deductible, keeps copays low, and removes any Part D late-enrollment penalty. People with Medicaid, Supplemental Security Income or a Medicare Savings Program qualify automatically; others apply through Social Security. State Medicare Savings Programs can also help pay the Part B premium.
facts.summary: Extra Help lowers Part D costs for people with limited income and removes the late-enrollment penalty; apply through Social Security.

facts.title: The yearly Open Enrollment Period
facts.question: When can people on Medicare change plans?
facts.text: Medicare Open Enrollment runs from October 15 to December 7 each year. During it, people already on Medicare can join, switch or drop a Medicare Advantage plan or a Part D drug plan, with the change starting January 1. Someone on Medicare Advantage also has a Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period from January 1 to March 31 to switch plans or return to Original Medicare. Medigap purchases follow separate rules and rights.
facts.summary: Open Enrollment is October 15 to December 7, with changes starting January 1.

facts.title: Original Medicare away from home
facts.question: Does Original Medicare work in another state?
facts.text: Original Medicare is accepted by any doctor or hospital in the United States that takes Medicare, in any state. Medicare Advantage plans have service areas and networks, so routine care in another state is often limited to emergencies or urgent care unless the plan has out-of-network benefits. Medigap policies travel with Original Medicare.
facts.summary: Original Medicare works with any U.S. provider who takes Medicare; Advantage plans usually limit routine care outside their area.
